papers.what_it_is: A benchmarking method for (quantum) reinforcement learning based on a sample-complexity estimator, applied to hybrid quantum and classical agents.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in their comparison of double deep Q learning and proximal policy optimization with their quantum counterparts, the quantum algorithm consistently outperforms the classical version when the number of trainable parameters is similar.
quotes: we found that the quantum algorithm consistently outperforms the classical version when the number of trainable parameters is similar.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical study on one new environment (BeamManagement6G) and one standard benchmark.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is conditioned on similar parameter count, not on the best classical model.

assertions.value: The authors report that the sample complexity of the classical models saturates once the hidden layer width reaches 64, while increasing the qubit number of the quantum model up to 14 does not show similar saturation.
quotes: the sample complexity of the classical models saturates once the hidden layer width reaches 64. In contrast, increasing the qubit number of the quantum model up to 14 does not exhibit a similar saturation behavior.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single study, one environment and algorithm (DDQN).

assertions.value: The authors state that despite extensive hyperparameter optimization they cannot guarantee that the quantum model was compared to the optimal classical one, and that currently no definitive statement on quantum advantage can be made.
quotes: we cannot guarantee that we compared the quantum model to the optimal classical one.
We argued that currently no definitive statement can be made but identified trends
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their own comparison (Section 7 and Section 8, p.9).

assertions.value: The authors state that their CartPole-v1 results should not be interpreted as evidence for quantum advantage, because the circuit sizes are very small and allow straightforward classical simulation.
quotes: We stress that these results should not be interpreted as evidence for quantum advantage. The circuit sizes are very small, allowing straightforward classical simulation
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their CartPole experiment (Section 6.4, p.8).

papers.title_in_file: A Novel Approach to Reduce Derivative Costs in Variational Quantum Algorithms
papers.what_it_is: A numerical and analytic resource comparison of the Quantum Non-Demolition Measurement (QNDM) method against direct measurement for estimating gradients and Hessians in variational quantum algorithms.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QNDM approach is more efficient than the direct-measurement approach, needing fewer resources to evaluate derivatives of a cost function.
quotes: We find that the QNDM approach is more efficient, i.e. it needs fewer resources, in evaluating the derivatives of a cost function.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation study (Qiskit) under the authors' resource model; no hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the cost comparison they fix the QNDM shot number at 500 and adjust the direct-measurement shot number for each instance so that the mean square errors of the two methods are equal.
quotes: we fix the number of shots for the QNDM approach is set to NQNDM = 500, while for the DM approach, the number of shots is adjusted for each instance to ensure MSEQNDM = MSEDM.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own comparison setup (Section V.B).

assertions.value: The authors anticipate that the QNDM advantage will further increase for more practical and complex problems, such as simulation of chemical compounds, molecules, or small quantum systems.
quotes: We anticipate that this advantage will further increase for more practical and complex problems, such as the simulation of chemical compounds, molecules, or small quantum systems
assertions.certainty_reason: An expectation stated without a run in the paper.

papers.title_in_file: Comparing Algorithms for Loading Classical Datasets into Quantum Memory
papers.what_it_is: A structured comparison of statevector-to-circuit state preparation algorithms on five quality attributes using a Pareto set over asymptotic complexity orders.

assertions.value: The authors report that their Pareto-set analysis reduces the compared algorithms to two dense and two sparse groups, highlighting inherent trade-offs.
quotes: Our analysis reduces the initial set of algorithms to two dense and two sparse groups, highlighting inherent trade-offs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The comparison uses complexity orders reported by the algorithm authors, with equal weights, and not runs.

assertions.value: The authors state that the algorithms under study represent a sample rather than an exhaustive set.
quotes: Thus, the algorithms under study represent a sample rather than an exhaustive set.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope (Section II).

assertions.value: The authors state that, for dense statevectors, the Pareto set of four groups can in practice be reduced to Zhang'21a and the family of Unitary algorithms, because the other two need a prohibitively large qubit count.
quotes: we can reduce this set to Zhang'21a and the family of Unitary algorithms. This reduction is due to the prohibitively large (even for future quantum computers) qubit count required for the other two algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: The reduction rests on the authors' reading of published complexity orders.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is impossible to achieve optimal levels of all quality attributes of state preparation simultaneously.
quotes: it is impossible to achieve optimal levels of all quality attributes simultaneously.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a general trade-off without a proof in the paper.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Machine Learning for Remote Sensing: Exploring Potential and Challenges
papers.what_it_is: A short review of QML for remote sensing with a small study of kernel value concentration in a quantum-kernel SVM.

assertions.value: The authors report that classical simulation time and estimated quantum runtime both start to grow exponentially around n = 15 qubits, and that the quantum runtime scaling is better than the classical one even with exponential concentration of kernel entries.
quotes: Both of the runtimes start to grow exponentially around number of qubits n = 15, but the crucial observation is that, even with the exponential concentration of kernel entries, the quantum runtime scaling is better than classical one.
Both TQ and TC scale exponentially, therefore there is no hope for quantum supremacy, where the classic and quantum algorithms are in different complexity classes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The quantum runtime comes from the authors' simple model, not a quantum run.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical time is measured; the quantum time is a model estimate.

assertions.value: The authors report that independent kernel entries of fidelity kernels with a ZZ feature map vanish exponentially with the number of qubits, shown on m = 100 artificially generated data points.
quotes: of independent kernel entries vanish exponentially with the number of qubits n used.
We show the kernel value concentration on m = 100 artificially generated data points.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single study on artificial data.

assertions.value: The authors acknowledge that their simple runtime model does not take into account the cost of quantum computation nor the effect of hardware noise.
quotes: we acknowledge that our simple model does not take into account the cost of quantum computation nor the effect of hardware noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their model (Section 4).

assertions.value: The authors postulate that quantum advantage has room at an intermediate size of quantum machines.
quotes: We postulate that in the intermediate size of quantum machines there is a room for quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: A postulate, not shown in the paper.

papers.title_in_file: In Search of Quantum Advantage: Estimating the Number of Shots in Quantum Kernel Methods
papers.what_it_is: A method for estimating the circuit runs needed in quantum kernel estimation, with a numerical study of exponential value concentration and a runtime and energy comparison with classical simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that the actual runtime of the quantum routines renders them impractical even for moderate-sized problems, and conclude that the utility of quantum kernel methods may not be as substantial as initially anticipated.
quotes: However, the actual runtime of the quantum routines renders them impractical, even for moderate-sized problems. Consequently, we may conclude that the versatility and utility of quantum kernel methods may not be as substantial as initially anticipated.
assertions.certainty_reason: Resource estimates from simulations on a few datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report expecting quantum utility for roughly n > 40 qubits in all presented cases, with possible utility found at n = 37 at the least.
quotes: In general, we expect quantum utility for roughly n > 40 in all the presented cases. We have found, that the possible utility is achieved with, at least, n = 37.
assertions.certainty_reason: Estimates for projected kernels on one dataset family and feature map.

assertions.value: The authors state that the numerical analysis was performed only for the binary classification task and for a limited number of datasets.
quotes: It was performed only for the binary classification task, for a limited number of datasets.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their own analysis (Section 5, p.14).

assertions.value: The authors state that they introduce two effects that necessitate more measurement precision through additional circuit runs: the spread effect and the concentration effect.
quotes: We introduce two critical effects that necessitate an increased measurement precision through additional circuit runs: the spread effect and the concentration effect.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines these effects (Abstract and Section 2).

papers.title_in_file: A Review of the Applications of Quantum Machine Learning in Optical Communication Systems
papers.what_it_is: A review of quantum and quantum-inspired machine learning algorithms for optical signal processing.

assertions.value: The authors state that the review surveys several proposed quantum and quantum-inspired machine learning algorithms and their applicability with current technology to optical signal processing.
quotes: In this review, we survey several proposed quantum and quantum-inspired machine learning algorithms and their applicability with current technology to optical signal processing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in the abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computers have not yet reached the efficiency and scalability to outperform classical computers for most ML tasks, especially for industrial deployment.
quotes: As of now, quantum computers have not reached the level of efficiency and scalability to outperform classical computers for most ML tasks, especially when considering an industrial deployment.
assertions.certainty_reason: A review statement without a single study behind it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classical data loading problem, a result of the unavailability of stable quantum memory, often introduces an exponential slowdown in hybrid quantum-classical QML implementations.
quotes: The classical data loading problem, a result of the unavailability of stable quantum memory, is a significant issue that often introduces an exponential slowdown in the hybrid
assertions.certainty_reason: A review statement without a result in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum advantage is still a questionable claim in many cases, especially for NISQ devices, despite demonstrations in some specific tasks.
quotes: While there have been some demonstrations of quantum advantage in specific tasks such as prime factorisation, it is still a questionable claim in many
assertions.certainty_reason: A review statement; no single study behind it.

papers.what_it_is: A linear-depth variational quantum algorithm for MaxCut, using quantum imaginary time evolution style updates, tested in simulation and on IonQ trapped-ion hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in numerical simulations targeting MaxCut, the algorithm consistently converges to optimal solutions.
quotes: We evaluate this ansatz in numerical simulations that target solutions to the MAXCUT problem.
With these innovations, the algorithm consistently converges to optimal solutions, with interesting highly-entangled dynamics along the way.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation study on instances the authors chose.

assertions.value: The authors report hardware runs on IonQ devices reaching optimal-solution probabilities with 24 or fewer qubits and 0.19 with 28 qubits, with the 32-qubit instance terminated early but still sampling the optimal solution.
assertions.anchor: Experimental Results on IonQ Aria and Forte, p.7
quotes: with 24 or fewer qubits and 0.19 with 28 qubits (execution of the 32-qubit instance was terminated early due to time constraints, but this still succeeded in sampling the optimal solution)
optimization of a truncated version of our ansatz with up to 32 qubits in a trapped-ion quantum computer
assertions.certainty_reason: A few hand-picked graph instances on one vendor's hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says without error mitigation, while the text says symmetrization error mitigation was used.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the hardware runs the ansatz was truncated to 60 parametrized two-qubit ZY gates.
assertions.anchor: Experimental Results on IonQ Aria and Forte, p.6
quotes: the ansatz (3) was truncated to 60 parametrized 2-qubit ZY gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own hardware setup (p.6).

assertions.value: The authors argue that their algorithm produces large amounts of entanglement, suggesting it will be unsimulatable at scale by conventional methods that represent limited entanglement.
quotes: We argue our algorithm produces large amounts of entanglement, suggesting it will be unsimulatable at scale when using conventional methods representing limited entanglement
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument from measured entropy, not a proof of classical hardness.

papers.title_in_file: AutoQC: Automated Synthesis of Quantum Circuits Using Neural Network
papers.what_it_is: A neural-network-guided search that synthesizes small quantum circuits from input-output pairs, evaluated on seven reversible-logic gate benchmarks.

assertions.value: The authors report that random search would take about 169 hours to generate a quantum circuit with four qubits and a quantum cost of 6, which they use as a baseline for how hard synthesis is.
quotes: it took about 169 hours to generate a quantum circuit with four qubits and a quantum cost of 6
assertions.certainty_reason: Estimated from a one-hour random search in the authors' environment.

assertions.value: The authors report that, except for TSG which failed to generate, their approach was faster than the previous study and achieved the lowest quantum cost, while noting that the environments differ and a simple time comparison is not possible.
quotes: However, except for TSG, which failed to generate, our approach was faster and achieved the lowest quantum cost.
Since the experimental environment is different from the previous study, a simple comparison of execution time is not possible.
assertions.certainty_reason: One study, small benchmark, different environments from the earlier work.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the larger-cost model they synthesized TSG in only one out of 100 trials.
quotes: we succeeded in synthesizing only one out of 100 trials.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single empirical result.

assertions.value: The authors state that even after a successful single trial they do not know whether the synthesized circuit is optimal, so a suitable circuit must be chosen after several trials.
quotes: The problem with our approach is that even if we succeed in synthesizing a quantum circuit in a single trial, we do not know if it is an optimal quantum circuit.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their approach (Section IV.B, p.6).
